[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

Healthcare applications generate high volumes of processing tasks — claim adjudication, eligibility checks, document processing, batch job execution — that must be distributed across multiple worker instances. Without a work queue, producers are tightly coupled to a single task executor, load balancing is absent, retry logic is ad hoc, and scaling the processing tier requires changing application code. Single-threaded, direct-invocation approaches become bottlenecks and single points of failure.
page_texts.5:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#solution-overview]

### Solution Overview

The Work Queue pattern uses a single shared queue to which multiple competing consumer workers subscribe — a topology also known as the Competing Consumers pattern. Each task message is delivered to exactly one worker. Workers acknowledge messages only after successful processing; if a worker crashes before acknowledging, the broker redelivers the message to another available worker. Failed tasks that cannot be recovered are routed to a Dead Letter Channel for investigation and replay.

Within the enterprise platform, Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ) is the supported broker implementation for this pattern. For enterprise-mandated configuration requirements — naming conventions, TLS, credential management, and compliance rules — see [STD-APP-EVT-007 — RabbitMQ Enterprise Messaging Standard](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).
page_texts.6:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#when-to-use]

### When to Use

- **Parallelizable Task Processing**: Claim adjudication, eligibility checks, document ingestion, and PDF extraction jobs that can be processed independently by any available worker
- **Load Balancing**: Distributing a stream of tasks evenly across a variable-size pool of workers, allowing the pool to scale horizontally without changing the producer
- **Decoupled Task Execution**: Separating task submission (producer) from task execution (worker) to allow independent deployment, scaling, and failure isolation
- **Retry and Fault Tolerance**: Tasks that may transiently fail and require automatic retry before routing to a DLQ for manual investigation
page_texts.7:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#when-not-to-use]

### When NOT to Use

- **Message Ordering Requirements**: When strict ordering within a processing domain is required, use a single consumer or a partitioned/sharded approach instead
- **Fan-Out Broadcasting**: When all consumers must receive a copy of each message, use the Publish-Subscribe pattern (PTN-APP-EVT-017) with a fanout or topic exchange
- **Request-Reply**: When the producer requires a synchronous response from the worker, use the Request-Reply pattern (PTN-APP-EVT-018)
- **Stateful Stream Processing**: When events must be correlated across a time window or against stateful aggregates, consider a stream processing approach
page_texts.8:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#benefits]

### Benefits

- **Horizontal Scalability**: Add or remove workers without changing producers or broker topology
- **Fair Work Distribution**: Prefetch count limits in-flight messages per worker, preventing fast workers from monopolizing the queue
- **Fault Isolation**: Worker crashes do not lose work; unacknowledged messages are requeued to another worker
- **Operational Visibility**: Queue depth, consumer count, and DLQ size provide clear operational signals
- **Decoupled Deployment**: Producers and workers deploy and scale independently

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#business-context]

### Business Context

Healthcare and human services platforms generate continuous streams of processing tasks that must be completed reliably within defined SLA windows. Examples include:

- **Claim Adjudication**: Hundreds to thousands of claim submissions per hour requiring rule-based validation, eligibility lookup, and adjudication decisions
- **Eligibility Determination**: Member eligibility checks triggered by enrollment events, provider requests, or scheduled batch runs
- **Document Processing**: Ingestion, OCR extraction, and indexing of uploaded documents (explanation of benefits, prior authorization requests, supporting clinical documentation)
- **Batch Job Execution**: Decomposed batch jobs where individual task units (record-level operations) can be processed concurrently by multiple workers

Business requirements include:

- **Reliability**: Tasks must not be silently dropped; every submitted task must either succeed or land in a recoverable error queue
- **SLA Compliance**: Regulatory and contractual deadlines require predictable throughput and the ability to scale worker capacity to meet demand spikes
- **Audit Trail**: All task processing activity must be traceable for compliance review
page_texts.11:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

The enterprise platform uses Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ) as the message broker for task queuing workloads. The Work Queue pattern applies equally to any broker that supports durable queues, at-least-once delivery, consumer acknowledgements, and dead-letter routing — including Kafka, ActiveMQ, and Azure Service Bus. The structural concepts in this pattern are broker-agnostic; AMQP-specific configuration details for the enterprise RabbitMQ implementation are found in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

**Current State Without Work Queues:**

- Producers directly invoke task executors via synchronous HTTP, creating tight coupling and eliminating independent scaling
- No load balancing: a single task executor becomes the bottleneck; adding capacity requires changing DNS, load balancer configuration, or producer code
- No standardized retry: transient failures (database timeouts, external service unavailability) cause immediate task loss or require custom retry loops baked into the producer
- No DLQ: permanently failed tasks disappear; operators have no visibility into failure rates or failure reasons
- Difficult to observe: no queue depth metric to signal backpressure or scaling needs
page_texts.12:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#problem-details]

### Problem Details

**Problem 1: Tight Producer-Consumer Coupling**

When producers call consumers directly, adding a second consumer requires the producer to implement its own load balancing or service discovery. Removing a consumer requires draining in-flight work from it before deployment. Producers must know the number and addresses of active workers.

**Problem 2: No Inherent Retry or Fault Tolerance**

Synchronous invocation provides no automatic retry for transient failures. If a worker crashes mid-task, the task is lost. Re-submitting tasks requires producer-side logic that is rarely implemented consistently across teams.

**Problem 3: Scaling is Disruptive**

Scaling task executor capacity requires either changing producer configuration or deploying a load balancer in front of workers. Neither approach allows workers to scale independently based on queue depth.

**Problem 4: No Operational Signal for Backpressure**

Without a queue, there is no observable signal indicating that task volume exceeds processing capacity. Operators have no leading indicator before SLA breaches occur.
page_texts.13:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#forces-and-constraints]

### Forces and Constraints

- **PHI Sensitivity**: Task payloads may include PHI. Routing metadata (queue names, routing keys) must not contain sensitive identifiers. Enterprise requirements for PHI handling, including TLS enforcement and connection security, are defined in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).
- **Idempotency**: At-least-once delivery semantics mean a message may be redelivered if a worker crashes after processing but before acknowledging. Task logic must handle redelivery safely — processing the same task twice must produce the same outcome.
- **Variable Processing Time**: Task processing time affects how in-flight message limits should be tuned. A fixed in-flight cap per worker prevents fast workers from accumulating a large backlog while slow workers sit idle.
- **Managed Broker Constraints**: The enterprise platform uses Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ). Topology declarations — exchanges, queues, bindings, and queue-level arguments — must be compatible with the managed service. Configuration specifics are defined in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#pattern-description]

### Pattern Description

The Work Queue pattern is built on three structural elements:

1. **Exchange / Router**: A durable routing mechanism that receives published task messages and routes them to the target queue by exact destination match. On the enterprise platform (RabbitMQ), this is a direct exchange. Exchange naming follows the domain convention defined in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

2. **Single Shared Queue**: A single durable queue bound to the exchange. All competing consumer workers read from this one queue, which ensures each task is dispatched to exactly one worker. Queue durability ensures the queue and its messages survive broker restarts. Queue naming follows the convention defined in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

3. **Competing Consumers**: Multiple worker instances share the same queue. The broker dispatches each message to one available consumer (round-robin by default), tempered by a per-consumer in-flight message limit that prevents fast workers from accumulating backlogs while slow workers sit idle.

**Dead Letter Channel:** A separate dead-letter exchange and queue receive messages that are explicitly rejected by a consumer after retry exhaustion. The source queue is configured to forward rejected messages to the dead-letter exchange automatically. Dead-lettered messages carry metadata about the failure (reason, timestamp, source queue, retry count) for operational investigation and replay.

**Key Design Principles:**

- Route by destination: routing key equals the queue name — explicit and inspectable
- Message persistence: messages are flagged for broker-persisted storage so they survive broker restarts
- Manual acknowledgement: messages are redelivered if a consumer disappears before acknowledging
- Per-consumer in-flight limit: controls how many unacknowledged messages a single worker holds at once
- Dead-letter TTL on DLQ: prevents unbounded DLQ growth; duration configured per domain SLA

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#components]

### Components

| Component | Responsibility | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Producer** | Publishes task messages to the exchange with destination key | Message persistence and PHI handling requirements per [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md) |
| **Exchange / Router** | Routes messages to the bound work queue by destination key match | Declared durable; shared across producers |
| **Work Queue** | Buffers tasks for competing workers; configured with dead-letter routing | Durable; dead-letter channel configured on the queue |
| **Worker Consumer** | Processes task messages; acknowledges on success, rejects on permanent failure | Must be idempotent; in-flight message limit tuned per workload |
| **Dead Letter Exchange** | Routes rejected messages to the DLQ | Separate exchange per domain |
| **Dead Letter Queue** | Holds permanently failed tasks for investigation and replay | Monitored; TTL configured to prevent unbounded growth |
page_texts.18:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#interactions]

### Interactions

**Happy Path:**

1. Producer declares exchange and queue (idempotent declarations — safe to run on every startup)
2. Producer publishes task message with destination routing key and persistent delivery flag
3. The exchange routes the message to the bound work queue
4. A worker with available in-flight capacity receives the message
5. Worker processes the task (e.g., runs adjudication logic, writes result to database)
6. Worker sends an acknowledgement — the broker removes the message from the queue

**Transient Failure with Retry:**

1. Worker receives message and processing fails with a transient error (database timeout, downstream service unavailable)
2. Worker catches the exception and calls `basic_nack(delivery_tag=..., requeue=True)` to requeue the message
3. RabbitMQ redelivers the message to an available worker (possibly the same worker)
4. After a configurable number of attempts, the worker calls `basic_nack(requeue=False)` — message is dead-lettered
5. RabbitMQ routes the message to the DLQ exchange and DLQ queue with `x-death` metadata appended

**Worker Crash (No ACK):**

1. Worker receives message but crashes before calling `basic_ack`
2. RabbitMQ detects channel/connection close; message is returned to the queue as ready
3. Another available worker receives and processes the message
4. No message loss occurs; idempotent worker logic handles potential redelivery safely
page_texts.19:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#variations]

### Variations

**Variation 1: Priority Queue**

Add `x-max-priority` to queue arguments to enable message priority (1-10). High-priority tasks (e.g., urgent prior authorization requests) preempt lower-priority tasks (e.g., routine batch jobs).

**Variation 2: Delayed Retry with x-delayed-message Plugin**

Instead of immediate requeue, use the `rabbitmq-delayed-message-exchange` plugin to implement exponential backoff between retries (e.g., 1s, 5s, 30s). Avoids tight retry loops on transiently unavailable downstream services.

**Variation 3: Per-Task-Type Queues**

When different task types have significantly different processing times or SLAs, declare separate work queues per task type (e.g., `eligibility.adjudication.tasks` and `eligibility.eligibility-check.tasks`). This prevents slow tasks from blocking fast tasks.

**Variation 4: Consumer Autoscaling**

Monitor queue depth (`messages_ready` metric from RabbitMQ management API or CloudWatch) and trigger Kubernetes HPA or KEDA-based autoscaling to add workers when depth exceeds threshold, and remove workers when depth returns to baseline.

- Experience with retry logic and dead letter queue handling

- Naming convention agreement per STD-APP-EVT-007

The enterprise implementation of this pattern uses Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ) as the broker. page_texts.23:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#conceptual-implementation-steps]

#### Conceptual Implementation Steps

At a pattern level, the implementation sequence is:

1. **Declare the exchange** (durable, point-to-point routing type) — idempotent, run on every startup
2. **Declare the work queue** (durable, with dead-letter routing configured) and bind it to the exchange
3. **Declare the dead-letter exchange and DLQ**, bind the DLQ to the dead-letter exchange
4. **Configure consumers** with an in-flight message limit; enable manual acknowledgement (not auto-ACK)
5. **Implement the message handler**: acknowledge on success; reject without requeue after retry exhaustion
6. **Publish messages** with persistence flag set and no PHI in the routing key

All naming conventions, specific argument names, and technology-specific configuration values are defined in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

> **For the complete RabbitMQ implementation example** including full topology setup, consumer worker, and producer — see [STD-APP-EVT-007 — RabbitMQ Enterprise Messaging Standard](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).
page_texts.24:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#best-practices]

### Best Practices

1. **Always Use Manual Acknowledgements**: Disable auto-acknowledgement so messages are only removed from the queue after the worker has successfully processed them. Auto-ACK causes silent task loss if a worker crashes during processing.

2. **Implement Idempotent Task Processing**: At-least-once delivery means a message may be delivered more than once. Workers must check whether a task was already completed (via an idempotency key on a domain-specific task identifier) before performing side effects.

3. **Tune the In-Flight Message Limit to Task Duration**: For long-running tasks (> 1 second), start with a limit of 1 and increase only after load testing. For sub-second tasks, higher limits (5–20) improve throughput. Set too high, fast workers will buffer large backlogs while slow workers sit idle.

4. **Monitor Queue Depth and DLQ Size**: Queue depth is the primary operational signal. A growing queue means insufficient consumer capacity. A growing DLQ indicates systematic processing failures requiring investigation.

5. **Declare Topology at Startup Idempotently**: Always declare exchanges, queues, and bindings on startup rather than relying on pre-provisioned topology. This ensures workers and producers are self-healing after broker restarts.

6. **Separate DLQ per Work Queue**: A shared DLQ makes it impossible to identify which workflow produced a failure. Each work queue should have its own isolated DLQ.

7. **Keep Routing Metadata Free of PHI**: Use opaque identifiers (member IDs, claim IDs) in routing keys and queue names. PHI belongs only in the message payload, which is protected in transit by TLS. See [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md) for enterprise PHI handling requirements.
page_texts.25:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

1. **Requeuing indefinitely without a retry limit**: A permanently failing message will loop back to the queue and consume worker capacity, blocking other tasks. Always track retry count using the broker's dead-letter metadata and route to the DLQ after a maximum retry count.

2. **Setting the in-flight limit too high for long tasks**: Workers with long processing times that hold many in-flight messages will appear "busy" to the broker while actual throughput is low. Other workers sit idle waiting for work. Start low and increase only after load testing.

3. **Not declaring topology idempotently at startup**: Relying on pre-provisioned topology means workers silently fail to consume after broker restarts that clear non-durable state.

4. **Omitting message persistence**: Without a persistence flag on published messages, messages are held in memory and lost on a broker restart even if the queue itself is durable.

5. **Including PHI in error log context**: When constructing error messages for logging or DLQ routing, ensure that PHI from the message payload is not included in log lines. Enterprise PHI handling requirements are in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

page_texts.28:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#compliance-requirements]

### Compliance Requirements

For the full set of mandatory compliance requirements applicable to the enterprise RabbitMQ implementation of this pattern, see [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md). Key areas include:

- **TLS**: All broker connections must use encrypted transport; plaintext connections are prohibited
- **PHI Handling**: PHI must not appear in routing keys, queue names, or log messages; payloads with PHI are protected in transit by TLS
- **Credential Management**: Broker credentials must be stored and rotated via AWS Secrets Manager
- **DLQ Requirement**: Every production queue must have a dead-letter channel configured; this is mandatory, not optional
- **Vhost Isolation**: Each domain operates in a dedicated virtual host; cross-domain routing uses the integration pattern (PTN-APP-EVT-013)

### Monitoring and Metrics

| Metric | Target | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Queue Depth** | < SLA threshold (TBD per domain) | Amazon MQ CloudWatch / RabbitMQ Management API |
| **Consumer Count** | ≥ 1 at all times | Amazon MQ CloudWatch |
| **DLQ Depth** | 0 (any value triggers investigation) | Amazon MQ CloudWatch / RabbitMQ Management API |
| **Message Processing Rate** | ≥ publish rate (queue draining or stable) | Application metrics |
| **In-Flight Message Count** | ≤ in-flight limit × worker count | Amazon MQ CloudWatch |

**Alerting Thresholds (pending calibration with domain owners):**

- **Critical**: Consumer count = 0 for > 2 minutes; DLQ depth > 10 messages
- **Warning**: Queue depth exceeds SLA-based threshold for > 5 minutes; DLQ depth > 0
- **Info**: Worker autoscaling event triggered; DLQ message detected

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#example-1-eligibility-adjudication-task-distribution]

### Example 1: Eligibility Adjudication Task Distribution

**Context:** An eligibility service receives hundreds of adjudication task requests per hour. Each task requires a database lookup, external rules engine call, and result persistence. Processing time varies from 200ms to 8 seconds. The service must scale to meet daily peaks while maintaining a 98% SLA for task completion within 15 minutes of submission.

**Topology:**

- Exchange: `eligibility.tasks` (direct, durable) per naming convention in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md)
- Queue: `eligibility.adjudication.tasks` (durable, dead-letter configured, TTL of 15 min)
- DLQ: `eligibility.adjudication.tasks.dlq`
- Workers: 3–10 instances (autoscaled via KEDA based on queue depth)
- In-flight limit: 2 per worker (long processing times; low value prevents buffering backlogs per worker)

**Task Payload (illustrative — no PHI in routing key):**

```json
{
  "taskId": "adj-20260406-00123",
  "taskType": "eligibility_check",
  "memberId": "M-987654",
  "requestedBy": "provider-portal",
  "submittedAt": "2026-04-06T14:32:00Z"
}
```

**Outcome:** Tasks distributed evenly across worker pool; workers scale from 3 to 8 during peak hours; DLQ captures ~0.02% of tasks failing due to rules engine unavailability; operators replay DLQ after rules engine recovery without data loss.

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#example-2-document-processing-pipeline]

### Example 2: Document Processing Pipeline

**Context:** Members upload supporting documents (PDFs, images) for prior authorization requests. Each document must be virus-scanned, OCR-extracted, classified, and stored. Processing time is 5–30 seconds per document.

**Topology:**

- Exchange: `documents.tasks` (direct, durable)
- Queue: `documents.processing.tasks` (durable, dead-letter configured)
- Workers: Dedicated document processing pods with in-flight limit of 1 (high per-task resource usage)

**Operational Notes:** Worker pods are resource-intensive (CPU for OCR); an in-flight limit of 1 ensures each worker holds at most one document at a time, preventing out-of-memory errors from concurrent processing of multiple large documents.
page_texts.35:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#scenario-1-batch-job-decomposition]

#### Scenario 1: Batch Job Decomposition

A nightly batch run produces 50,000 individual record-processing tasks. Rather than processing sequentially in a single job, the batch orchestrator publishes all 50,000 tasks to the work queue. 20 worker pods process tasks in parallel, completing the batch in 1/20th the sequential time. Workers scale down after batch completion.
page_texts.36:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#scenario-2-graceful-degradation-under-load-spikes]

#### Scenario 2: Graceful Degradation Under Load Spikes

A claim submission spike during open enrollment doubles the task volume. Queue depth grows as existing workers fall behind. A KEDA autoscaler detects queue depth exceeding the threshold and adds 5 additional worker pods. Queue depth stabilizes; new workers are removed after the spike subsides. No tasks are lost and no code changes are required.
page_texts.37:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#scenario-3-dlq-investigation-and-replay]

#### Scenario 3: DLQ Investigation and Replay

A downstream rules engine API upgrade introduces a breaking change, causing 150 adjudication tasks to fail and route to the DLQ. Platform engineers identify the issue, deploy a fixed worker, then replay the 150 DLQ messages by republishing them to the work queue. All 150 tasks process successfully on replay.

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md#tldr]

## TL;DR

**Problem:** High-volume task workloads (claim adjudication, document processing, batch job execution) need to be distributed across multiple worker instances for parallel processing, fault tolerance, and independent scaling — but direct producer-to-consumer invocation creates tight coupling, no load balancing, and no automatic retry.

**Solution:** Publish tasks to a durable work queue shared by multiple competing consumer workers. Each message is delivered to exactly one worker. Manual acknowledgement after successful processing ensures no task is lost on worker crash. Failed tasks route to a dead-letter channel after retry exhaustion. On the enterprise platform, Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ) is the broker; see [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md) for all configuration requirements.

**When to Use:**

- Parallelizable task processing (claim adjudication, eligibility checks, document processing)
- Load-balanced task distribution across a horizontally scalable worker pool
- Decoupling task producers from task executors for independent deployment and scaling
- Workloads requiring at-least-once delivery with dead-letter recovery for failed tasks

**Key Benefits:**

- Each message delivered to exactly one worker — no duplicate processing at the queue level
- Manual acknowledgement guarantees no task loss on worker crash
- Per-worker in-flight message limit provides fair work distribution across variable-speed workers
- Dead-letter channel captures permanently failed tasks for investigation and replay without data loss
- Worker pool scales independently of producers

**Implementation Complexity:** Low to Medium

**Prerequisites:** Amazon MQ (RabbitMQ) instance, virtual host provisioned per domain per [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md), TLS-enabled broker endpoint, broker credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, idempotent task processing logic

**Related Patterns:** PTN-APP-EVT-017 (Publish-Subscribe), PTN-APP-EVT-018 (Request-Reply), PTN-APP-EVT-019 (Dead Letter Channel), PTN-INFRA-EVT-001 (DLQ Pattern)
